rv.q: It Hot is a delight from start to finish.
“It Hot,” which opened at the Shubert Theatre tonight, manages to speak to the moment with sizzle, polish and expert understanding of how to please a crowd.
What could have been a dated drag farce ends up as a show that many will like immensely — a musical filled with fun, energy and heart.

That’s a pretty high standard, after all, and in its staging (by Casey Nicholaw), its revamped plot (by Matthew López and Amber Ruffin) and especially its songs (by Marc Shaiman and Scott Wittman), “It Hot” clears the bar handily.
You'll leave this show with a smile on your face, and why not?
This fizzy adaptation of the Billy Wilder film classic is a crowd-pleasing musical that knows how to work an audience
The show is a fizzy, feel-good entertainment that delivers plenty of laughs and some unexpectedly touching moments.
Without it, there is no surprise, intellectually or emotionally, and that is the case here, even though that original film was full of shocks and wonders.
By the end of it, all I could think is, Well, this is most of the way to being an incredible musical.
And in this silly, woozy, pretty show, with its endless tap numbers, it doesn’t exactly fit.
However, even if you go in totally cold — “Who’s Jack Lemmon?” God forbid — the show still disappoints as a stand-alone piece of theater.
Whether you like it hot, cold, or even in the pot, nine days old, you’re probably going to like this show.
If you’re a sucker for fast-paced glamour executed in high style, this is the one for you.
It Hot has everything a Broadway musical should have: a superb cast, a great score, terrific choreography and the highest production values.
It Hot is a wildly entertaining farce from start to finish.
I imagine you'll make your own connections while viewing what is sure to be Broadway's next huge hit.

And yet here comes It Hot, blazing a three-alarm fire with charm and wit to remind us of the joys that beautiful people, electric performances, exciting choreography and foot-stomping, finger-snapping, neck-pulsing music can inspire.
That’s correct, if not exactly thrilling theater.
It Hot finds new vigor in roaring, raucous musical comedy.
It Hot is a booze-soaked, boisterous good time from start to finish.

With the exception of the lively title song, Marc Shaiman and Scott Wittman’s (“Hairspray”) big band-style score is derivative and serviceable at best. But taken on the whole, 'It Hot' is more than worth celebrating.
By delivering its pointed messages with such virtuosity and sheer spunk, “It Hot” manages to burn more brightly than most musicals of its kind.
...Natasha Katz’s warm lighting create the perfect atmosphere for this joyfully ridiculous show. Despite its occasional lapses into preachiness, it’s a really Hot time.

Indeed, acceptance is the key to just sitting back in your seat and embracing all the great stuff onstage in “It Hot” -- even if this overstuffed show sometimes feels that it should have been renamed “A Lot.”
For the most part, It Hot succeeds in its aim of simply entertaining its audiences with those two most glorious words in the English language.
If you're thirsty for an old-fashioned, energetic mega-musical with new-fashioned stars and sensibilities, then It Hot satisfies on all counts.
Whatever puzzles there are in story and character in the Broadway show are swept along by the wonderful dancing and music that keeps the show rattling along.
Never has more been way too much.
Whether you leave feeling entertained or overwhelmed probably depends on how eager you are for a fun time.
The music by Marc Shaiman and lyrics by Scott Wittman and Shaiman are smart and enhance the story, not just dropped in for a pause.
Well, you could have knocked me over with a feather because I will forgive the flaws of It Hot as a theatrical experience to embrace the overwhelming authenticity.
Its creators desire to not offend anybody is actually more offensive than they think, tiptoeing when they should land with both feet hard.

cn.t: Critics praise this fizzy, crowd-pleasing adaptation for its energetic choreography and fresh updates to the film classic's gender politics, though some find the modernization heavy-handed and the razzle-dazzle exhausting.

vs.sum: The Shubert Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions, though some seats may require leaning forward for a full view. The sound quality is generally consistent and clear. While legroom is limited in some areas, the theater's historic charm and central location add to its appeal. Facilities are average, with typical lines at restrooms and concessions.

acc.note: 7 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No wheelchair-accessible restrooms (available across street).
